288.title: One hand
288.hook: Hakuin's koan: you know the sound of two hands; what is the sound of one
288.carry: listen for what's under the noise
288.howItsDone: In Japanese Rinzai Zen, Hakuin's 'sound of one hand' is one of the first koans a teacher may assign, often alongside or instead of mu, followed by a series of checking questions in private interviews.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ordinary mind, and your line, nothing useless clings to the mind. Today, a question you've probably heard before.
screen: `ORDINARY MIND — NOTHING USELESS CLINGS TO THE MIND.`

segments.voice: You've heard it, probably in a cartoon, or from a friend being clever at a party: what's the sound of one hand clapping? It's become a punch line, shorthand for a question so deep it's silly. Somebody waves one hand in the air, and everybody laughs. But the question has a real home and a real author: a Japanese monk who lived in a small, poor temple at the foot of Mount Fuji, painted wild ink pictures, and nearly broke his own health with practice when he was young.
screen: `A PUNCH LINE AT A PARTY.` → `ONE HAND WAVED IN THE AIR.` → `A REAL HOME, A REAL AUTHOR.`

segments.voice: His name was Hakuin Ekaku, and he lived from 1686 to 1769. He's remembered as the teacher who revived Rinzai Zen in Japan when it had grown sleepy; almost every Rinzai teacher in Japan today traces their line through him. For years Hakuin gave his students mu, Zhaozhou's dog, as their first koan. Then, late in life, he started giving them a question of his own. In a letter written in his late sixties, he explains it roughly like this: clap two hands together and there's a sound. What is the sound of one hand? He wrote that this question raised the great doubt in students more easily than mu. Notice what it does to you. The thinking mind reaches for an answer and finds nothing to grab. One hand makes no sound; any fool knows that. So what is he asking? The koan pushes attention toward listening itself, toward what's here before any sound, the silence every sound comes out of and goes back into. Students work with it for months, sometimes years, and teachers follow up with more questions: hear the sound of one hand from the soles of your feet, or stop the sound of one hand. Hakuin never meant it as a joke, but he had a big sense of humor; his paintings of monks and gods are full of it. He'd probably laugh at the party version too. Then he'd ask you to listen.
screen: `HAKUIN, WHO REVIVED RINZAI.` · `AFTER YEARS OF MU.` · `TWO HANDS MAKE A SOUND.` · `LISTENING ITSELF.` · then, large: `ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: First, just listen to whatever sounds are here: traffic, a fan, a bird, your own breath. Then notice the silence those sounds rise out of and fall back into, and rest there. If you like, lift one hand a little and ask: what is the sound of this? Don't answer; just listen.
One hand. Hakuin's koan: two hands clap and there's a sound; what is the sound of one hand?
Your line: listen for what's under the noise. The silence was there before the first sound. See you tomorrow.

289.title: Carrying a koan
289.hook: Rinzai students hold a koan all day and bring it to the teacher in private
289.howItsDone: Rinzai Zen students receive a koan from their teacher, hold it in sitting and daily work, and present their response in private interviews called dokusan or sanzen, several times a day during retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one hand, and your line, listen for what's under the noise. Today, what people actually do with a koan.
screen: `ONE HAND — LISTEN FOR WHAT'S UNDER THE NOISE.`

segments.voice: A song gets stuck in your head. Nobody decides to keep it. It just rides along: in the shower, on the drive, while you answer email, humming underneath everything else. Koan practice does that on purpose, not with a song but with a question like mu or the sound of one hand, carried through breakfast, work and the walk home. For two weeks you've been reading koans. But that isn't how people practice with them. It isn't done in an armchair.
screen: `A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `CHOSEN ON PURPOSE.` → `NOT IN AN ARMCHAIR.`

segments.voice: In Rinzai Zen, a student doesn't pick a koan off a shelf. The teacher gives it, usually mu or the sound of one hand to begin. Then the student carries it. In sitting meditation, the koan is the whole practice: not thinking about it, but becoming absorbed in it, breath after breath. And, the part that surprises people, it doesn't stay on the cushion. It goes to the kitchen, the garden, the walk between buildings. Hakuin, from yesterday, taught that practice in the middle of activity is far stronger than practice in stillness. Korean Seon teachers say the same about the hwadu: hold it while walking, standing, sitting and lying down. Several times a day during a retreat, and regularly the rest of the year, the student goes alone to the teacher's room. This private meeting is called dokusan, or sanzen. The student bows and presents the koan, not with an explanation but with a response: sometimes a word, a gesture, a silence. Often the teacher rings a small hand bell and the meeting is over. Not yet; go back and keep going. Some students hear that bell for months. By custom, what happens in the room stays in the room; students don't share their answers. That's one reason the published books of answers miss the point: a response only counts if it comes from you, in the moment, face to face. Passing the first koan doesn't end the work. Many more follow, each opening the first seeing a little wider.
screen: `THE TEACHER GIVES THE KOAN.` · `OFF THE CUSHION, INTO THE DAY.` · `ALONE IN THE TEACHER'S ROOM.` · `A SMALL BELL: NOT YET.` · then, large: `CARRY IT.`

segments.voice: Bring back mu, the first koan, and let it ride the out-breath the way you did eleven days ago: not thinking about it, just the sound, all the way out. Then imagine standing up and carrying it into one chore, the dishes, folding clothes, the walk to the mailbox, mu with each step, each plate.

Your line: carry it. On the cushion, and off it, all day long. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

290.title: What koans are not
290.hook: not riddles with clever answers; Soto Zen stresses just sitting instead, and both are Zen
290.howItsDone: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit shikantaza, usually facing a wall, without a koan; in Rinzai Zen they usually sit facing into the room and work with koans. Some lineages teach both.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dokusan, and your line, carry it. Today is the last day of the koans.

After two weeks of dogs, bowls, foxes, fingers, flags, flowers, faces, cats, good days and one hand, you might think Zen is basically koans. Step into a Soto Zen hall in Japan and there's something different. People sitting facing a plain wall. No question to hold. No interview bell. Just sitting, for a long time, very still. That's Zen too. Today the koans close with what they aren't, and with the other great way Zen is practiced.
screen: `DOGS, BOWLS, FOXES, FLAGS.` → `PEOPLE FACING A PLAIN WALL.` → `THAT'S ZEN TOO.`

segments.voice: First, what koans are not. They're not riddles with clever answers; the teacher's bell sends clever answers back. They're not nonsense meant to confuse you; each grew out of a real encounter and points somewhere. And they're not the only way to practice Zen. In Japan the two main Zen schools are Rinzai, which you've been meeting, and Soto. Soto was brought from China by a Japanese monk named Dogen. His teacher in China had a phrase for the heart of practice: just sitting. In Japanese, shikantaza. You sit upright, usually facing a wall, eyes half open, and you don't hold a koan, count breaths or aim at anything. You just sit, fully awake to sitting. Remember nothing to attain, from the Heart Sutra: Dogen taught that sitting isn't a means to awakening later. Sitting is awakening, being expressed. The difference isn't new. In Song-dynasty China, Dahui championed working on a single koan phrase, while Hongzhi taught a quiet practice he called silent illumination. They disagreed, and were friends: tradition says Hongzhi asked Dahui to handle his funeral. Today Rinzai teachers stress koans, Soto teachers stress just sitting, and both schools say the other is Zen. Soto teachers study koans too; Dogen wrote about them often. And some lineages, especially in the West, teach both. Two weeks of koans, closed in silence: don't solve it, mu, wash your bowl, not blind to cause, your own finger, mind moves, the smile, before you were born, sandals on the head, every day is a good day, ordinary mind, one hand, carry it. And now, just sitting.
screen: `NOT RIDDLES, NOT NONSENSE.` · `SOTO ZEN AND DOGEN.` · `SHIKANTAZA: JUST SITTING.` · `DAHUI AND HONGZHI, FRIENDS.` · then, large: `JUST SITTING.`

segments.voice: No koan, no counting, no word on the breath: sit upright as if a thread were lifting the crown of your head, eyes resting half open on the floor or a wall a little in front of you. When thoughts come, don't follow them and don't push them away; let them pass like weather. Just this body, sitting, breathing.
Shikantaza. Just sitting, facing a wall, holding no koan and aiming at nothing: the other great way Zen is practiced.
Your line: just sitting. Nothing to solve, nothing to add. That's two weeks of koans, closed.

291.title: The way of the elders
291.hook: the Buddhism of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, with the Pali canon as scripture
291.howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks walk an alms round at dawn, lay people offer food and visit temples on full-moon days, and the Pali canon is chanted in the original language in daily services.

segments.voice: Yesterday the koans closed with shikantaza, and your line, just sitting. Today, a new part of the path: the way of the elders.

Dawn in Luang Prabang, in Laos. A line of monks in saffron robes walks barefoot down a quiet street, bowls held in front of them. People kneel on mats by the curb and place a little sticky rice in each bowl. No one speaks. Much the same happens in towns across Thailand, Myanmar and Cambodia, and in a different form in Sri Lanka. Tradition says it has gone on for many centuries. After more than three weeks with the Heart Sutra and Zen, the next two go south and west, into the school that names itself for the elders.
screen: `DAWN IN LUANG PRABANG.` → `MONKS, BOWLS, STICKY RICE.` → `A SCHOOL NAMED FOR THE ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Theravada. Thera means an elder, a senior monk; vāda, a teaching, a way of speaking. The teaching of the elders. The name carries a claim: this is the Buddha's teaching as the senior monks remembered and recited it after his death, kept as closely as possible ever since. Theravada is the main Buddhism of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, with communities in Bangladesh, southern Vietnam, and cities all over the world. Its scripture is the Pali canon, written in Pali, an ancient Indian language close to the ones the Buddha spoke. How did it get south? The Sri Lankan chronicles tell it this way. The Indian emperor Ashoka, whose own inscriptions speak of his remorse after a bloody war, sent his son, a monk named Mahinda, to the king of Sri Lanka. The king listened and became a follower. Ashoka's daughter, the nun Sanghamitta, came later, bringing a branch of the tree the Buddha sat under. Tradition says a tree grown from it still stands at Anuradhapura, where pilgrims honor it today. Later, the chronicle says, monks in Sri Lanka wrote the canon down for the first time, fearing it could be lost. From there it traveled to Southeast Asia. Theravada and Mahayana Buddhists share the core: the four truths, the eightfold path, the three refuges. Where they differ, i'll say who says what.

292.title: Three baskets
292.hook: discipline, discourses, and the higher teaching: the Pali canon
292.howItsDone: Theravada monks memorize and chant passages from the three baskets, recite the monastic rules every two weeks, and in Myanmar monks can sit formal exams on the canon.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Theravada, and your line, still walking at dawn. Today, the scripture the elders kept.

In Mandalay, in Myanmar, a pagoda is surrounded by small white shrines, row after row, like a quiet city. Inside each one stands a marble slab, taller than a person, carved on both sides with tiny letters. Walk them all and you've walked through a book. A Burmese king had the whole scripture of his tradition carved in stone, slab after slab, so it would outlast palm leaves and paper. A book made of marble. What's carved there comes in three parts.
screen: `A CITY OF WHITE SHRINES.` → `MARBLE SLABS, BOTH SIDES CARVED.` → `A BOOK MADE OF MARBLE.`

segments.voice: Tipitaka. Ti, three. Piṭaka, basket. The three baskets. Nobody is completely sure why baskets. One old explanation pictures workers on a building site passing baskets of earth from hand to hand, the way the teaching passed from teacher to student by memory before it was written. The first basket is the Vinaya, the discipline: the rules for monks and nuns and, charmingly, the stories behind them, what happened that made the Buddha say, from now on, don't do that. The second is the Suttas, the discourses: the Buddha's talks and conversations, in five collections. The long ones, the middle-length ones, the connected ones grouped by topic, the numbered ones grouped by how many items they list, and a fifth collection of shorter works. That fifth one holds the Dhammapada, which this path has quoted before. One of its verses sums up the whole in Max Müller's English: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." The third basket is the Abhidhamma, the higher teaching: seven books that analyze the mind and experience into their tiniest moments, like a chemistry of consciousness. Theravada Buddhists study it seriously, and in Myanmar it's especially honored. Printed, the three baskets fill a long shelf. A British scholar, T. W. Rhys Davids, founded the Pali Text Society to publish and translate them, and his own translations are among those this path draws on.

Go around a few times, then let the names go and notice this moment of mind, the one the third basket tries to describe.

293.title: The forest monks
293.hook: the Thai forest tradition: monks in the jungle, keeping the old rules closely
293.howItsDone: In Thai forest monasteries in Thailand and abroad, monks eat one meal a day from the alms bowl, practice walking and sitting meditation, and keep the monastic rules strictly; lay visitors often come to stay and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tipitaka, and your line, a book made of marble. Today, monks who went back to the trees.

So much of the Buddha's life happened under trees. He was born, the story goes, in a grove, his mother holding a branch. He woke up under a tree. He gave his first teaching in a deer park. He died lying between two trees in a forest. The early monks lived in forests, slept at the roots of trees, and walked into villages only to collect food. Over the centuries many monasteries moved into towns and cities, and that's natural. But about a hundred years ago, in the northeast of Thailand, a handful of monks walked back into the jungle.
screen: `BORN IN A GROVE.` → `AWAKE UNDER A TREE.` → `BACK INTO THE JUNGLE.`

segments.voice: The best-known was Ajahn Mun, born in 1870 in Isan, the region of Thailand near the Lao border. Ajahn means teacher. With his own teacher, Ajahn Sao, he chose a hard life: wandering on foot through the forests of Thailand and Laos, sleeping under a cloth tent hung with a mosquito net, meditating through the night, and keeping the monastic rules as closely as the old texts describe. The forests then were full of tigers, snakes and malaria. The practice has an old name, dhutanga, a set of voluntary austerities listed in the commentaries: eating one meal a day, eating only from the bowl, living at the foot of a tree. Monks who took up the wandering life were called thudong monks, from that word. Ajahn Mun trained a generation of students. One of them, Ajahn Chah, founded a forest monastery in 1954 near the city of Ubon, and later a monastery for foreign monks. Through his students, forest monasteries now stand in England, Australia, New Zealand, the United States and beyond, where monks still walk for alms in the morning. Ajahn Chah liked to compare a trained mind to a still forest pool, where all kinds of wild animals come to drink, and you can watch them clearly. Most of the forests Ajahn Mun walked through have since been cut down. The monasteries became islands of trees. And the tradition keeps a simple conviction: the Buddha's teaching began in the forest, and the forest remembers.
screen: `AJAHN MUN WALKS INTO THE FOREST.` · `DHUTANGA: THE OLD AUSTERITIES.` · `AJAHN CHAH AND THE STILL POOL.` · `MONASTERIES AS ISLANDS OF TREES.` · then, large: `THE FOREST REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Picture a forest monastery: a clearing among tall trees, a simple wooden hall open on the sides, a swept path where a monk walks slowly back and forth, cicadas, a distant bird, cool early air. Then let the picture fade and imagine your mind as a still forest pool. Thoughts come to drink like animals at the edge; you don't chase them, you watch.
Arañña. The forest: where the Thai forest monks, following Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah, kept the old rules closely, deep among the trees.
Your line: the forest remembers. Watch the pool; don't chase what comes to drink. Day two hundred ninety-three.

294.title: The 227 rules
294.hook: a fully ordained monk keeps 227 rules, a nun more; rules as a shelter
294.howItsDone: Theravada monks keep the 227 rules of the Pāṭimokkha, confess lapses to one another and recite the rules together every new and full moon; lay Buddhists keep five precepts, and eight on observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arañña, the forest monks, and your line, the forest remembers. Today closes the week with the rules monks keep.

Rules are complicated. Speed limits, dress codes, the terms and conditions nobody reads. Rules can feel like a fence someone else built around you. A Theravada monk chooses, freely, to live by two hundred twenty-seven of them. Not eating after noon. Not touching money. Not digging in the ground. Not sleeping in a luxurious bed. That's the life of a fully ordained monk, and some keep it their whole lives. Why would anyone want that? The tradition's answer changes what a rule is.
screen: `SPEED LIMITS AND DRESS CODES.` → `TWO HUNDRED TWENTY-SEVEN, BY CHOICE.` → `WHAT A RULE IS.`

segments.voice: Vinaya means discipline, or training. It's the first of the three baskets. At its center is a list called the Pāṭimokkha: two hundred twenty-seven rules for monks in the Theravada tradition, and three hundred eleven for fully ordained nuns. Four are the gravest, called defeats: sexual intercourse, stealing, killing a human being, and falsely claiming spiritual attainments. Break one and you're no longer a monk. Most of the rest are small, and many have wonderful origin stories. The rule against digging the ground exists because of the small creatures living in the soil. Every two weeks, on the new moon and the full moon, the monks of a monastery gather, confess any lapses to each other, and one of them recites the whole list aloud. The Vinaya gives the Buddha's own reasons for making rules, ten of them, including the well-being of the community, its ease, restraint for the difficult, and the confidence of people who see monks living well. So the rules work less like a fence and more like a shelter: they keep the weather out so the practice can happen inside. About nuns: in Sri Lanka the Theravada line of fully ordained nuns died out centuries ago. In recent decades, ordinations have revived it, and some Sri Lankan and Western Theravadins recognize those nuns. The official monastic councils of Thailand and Myanmar do not yet. Look back at the week: one hand, carry it, just sitting, the way of the elders, three baskets, the forest remembers. And rules as a shelter.
screen: `VINAYA: DISCIPLINE, TRAINING.` · `FOUR DEFEATS AND MANY SMALL RULES.` · `RECITED AT EVERY NEW AND FULL MOON.` · `A SHELTER, NOT A FENCE.` · then, large: `RULES AS A SHELTER.`

segments.voice: Choose one small rule just for yourself, nothing heroic: no phone at the table, no second helping, not interrupting, no complaining until noon. Picture it not as a fence but as a small roof over your day, keeping something out so something else can grow, and breathe under that roof.
Vinaya. The monastic discipline: two hundred twenty-seven rules for Theravada monks, kept as a shelter for practice.
Your line: rules as a shelter. Weather stays out, practice grows in. That's the week.
